content.text: I have what I need. Every quoted span was located verbatim in the XML on re-reading, which settles the `quote_not_located` marker globally.

headline.statement: The pilot study's headline mood test, F(2, 42) = 18.44, cannot be produced by the three means and standard deviations printed in the same sentence, which imply an F between 26.0 and 27.0 under every group-size allocation tested.
headline.evidence: "A one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) revealed that the mood manipulation significantly affected participant mood, F(2, 42) = 18.44, p < .001. Participants in the positive mood condition reported more positive mood (M = 7.20, SD = .93) that those in the control condition (M = 6.15, SD = .52) ... Participants in the negative mood condition reported more negative mood (M = 4.98, SD = .98)" (N = 45, three conditions, error df 42). Achievable F at 15/15/15: [26.01, 27.04]; at 12/21/12: [23.95, 24.93]; at 9/27/9: [21.16, 22.06]. Reported F = 18.44 lies below all three, and 0 of 5,000 Monte Carlo draws reproduce it.
headline.plain: In the study that sets up the whole paper, the authors report a test result showing their happy/sad writing task changed people's mood. Working backwards from the average scores they print in the very same sentence, that test result should have been about 26; they print 18.44. Changing how many people were assumed to be in each group does not fix it, so one of the numbers in that sentence is not the number the analysis actually produced.

findings.title: Pilot mood ANOVA F of 18.44 lies below every F achievable from the three means and SDs printed beside it
findings.location: Pilot study, Results (mood manipulation ANOVA)
findings.reported: "A one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) revealed that the mood manipulation significantly affected participant mood, F(2, 42) = 18.44, p < .001." Group means/SDs in the same passage: 7.20 (.93), 6.15 (.52), 4.98 (.98); N = 45, three conditions.
findings.computed: rivets_anova, re-run at this stage: achievable F interval [26.01, 27.04] at n = 15/15/15, with 0 of 5,000 Monte Carlo draws over the rounding box reaching 18.44. Re-run at 12/21/12 gives [23.95, 24.93] and at 9/27/9 gives [21.16, 22.06]; the reported value sits below all three. The reported p (< .001) is not refuted -- every achievable F is MORE significant than the one printed, so the direction of the discrepancy is conservative.
findings.assumptions: Cell ns are not printed. n = 15 per group follows from N = 45 across three conditions with error df 42 (= 45 - 3), and the finding was deliberately re-tested at two progressively more unequal allocations to check that the assumption is not doing the work; it is not. The two t-tests reported in the same passage, t(42) = 3.43 and t(42) = -3.80, carry df 42, i.e. they are contrasts on the ANOVA's pooled error term rather than two-sample tests -- a two-sample recomputation of them therefore does not apply and is not offered here as evidence.
findings.reproduction: metascience rivets-anova --means 7.20,6.15,4.98 --sds 0.93,0.52,0.98 --ns 15,15,15 --reported-f 18.44 --reported-p 0.001 --p-is-threshold --decimals-mean 2 --decimals-sd 2 --decimals-f 2

consequence.explanation: The pilot's claim that the mood induction worked rests on a statistic that does not follow from the data printed beside it; the significance decision itself is unaffected, since every achievable F is more extreme than the reported one.

findings.plain: The pilot study reports an average mood score for each of three groups, and then a test statistic summarising how different those three averages are. The averages and the test statistic do not match: the averages imply a value around 26, and the paper prints 18.44. This holds whether the groups were equal-sized or badly unbalanced. The mismatch runs in the direction that makes the result look weaker, not stronger, so it is not the shape an exaggeration would take -- but one of the two sets of numbers is wrong.

findings.title: Sixty of Experiment 4's 193 stated participants appear in no reported analysis, with no exclusions or attrition disclosed
findings.location: Experiment 4, Participants and design versus Results and discussion
findings.reported: "University (N = 193, 103 female) students participated in the study for monetary compensation. This experiment used a 2(mood: positive, neutral) x 2 (direction of comparison: upward vs. downward) x 2(load: load vs. no load) factorial design, with an additional no mood induction, no comparison, no load control condition." Every factorial test is reported at error df 110; every contrast against the control at df 124.
findings.computed: check_summation_batch, re-run at this stage over all four experiments. Experiment 4: error df 110 + 8 cells = 118 in the factorial, contrast df 124 + 9 groups = 133 in total, against a stated N of 193 -- a shortfall of 60, 31% of the sample. The same arithmetic reconciles EXACTLY in the other three: Experiment 1 (43 + 4 = 47), Experiment 2 (126 + 15 = 141), Experiment 3 (88 + 8 = 96). 1 of 4 rows inconsistent.
findings.assumptions: The derivation assumes the two df values come from the models the Methods describe -- a 2x2x2 factorial and single-df contrasts against a hanging control -- which is what the paper states, and is the reading under which the other three experiments reconcile to the digit. Innocent explanations that would resolve it entirely and are stated nowhere in the paper: undisclosed exclusions, listwise deletion, or a typo in the reported N.
findings.reproduction: metascience summation --values 118,15 --expected-sum 193 --decimals 0,0 --tolerance 0 --description 'Experiment 4 participants implied by ANOVA error df 110 plus control cell implied by contrast df 124, against the reported N of 193'

consequence.explanation: Every Experiment 4 test runs on a subset roughly two-thirds the size of the sample the paper says it recruited, and the paper reports no exclusions, attrition or missing data anywhere in that experiment.

findings.plain: Experiment 4 says it recruited 193 students. The technical details attached to every one of its statistical tests imply that only about 133 people were actually in those analyses. The paper never mentions anyone dropping out, being excluded, or having missing data. The same check reconciles perfectly for the paper's other three experiments, so this is not a quirk of how the tests were counted -- roughly a third of Experiment 4's participants are simply unaccounted for.

findings.title: Two Table 2 self-evaluation cells report a standard deviation no whole-number responses can produce
findings.location: Table 2, Self-evaluation row, Positive/Unambiguous columns (Experiment 3)
findings.reported: "6.58 (.52)" and "4.08 (.52)" -- the Positive/Unambiguous upward and downward cells, on a self-rated attractiveness item the paper describes as a single seven-point scale.
findings.computed: grimmer_check, re-run at this stage on both cells at n = 12: the single GRIM-consistent total (79 for 6.58, 49 for 4.08) admits no integer sum-of-squares of the required parity that rounds to SD = 0.52, under either the sample (n-1) or population (n) convention, with or without the scale bounds. R rsprite2 independently rejects both cells with 'The standard deviation is not consistent with this mean and number of observations (fails GRIMMER test)'. The two engines agree. Denominator: 4 of 24 checks across the 16 Table 2 cells were flagged; all 16 cell means pass GRIM.
findings.assumptions: The cell n of 12 is derived, not printed: N = 96 in a 2x2x2 design with error df 88 (= 96 - 8) forces 12 per cell. Severity is capped at `suspicious` rather than `impossible` because the tool's discreteness premise was left at 'assumed' -- if each participant really contributed one whole-number rating on a seven-point item, as the paper's cross-reference implies, the arithmetic would license a stronger verdict, but that premise reaches Experiment 3 by cross-reference rather than by a scale printed in that section. R's refusal is likewise capped at `indeterminate` by our wrapper, because a raised exception is not a proof of infeasibility (measured false-raise rate 16.2%); it corroborates without licensing escalation.
findings.reproduction: metascience grimmer --mean 6.58 --sd 0.52 --n 12 --scale-min 1 --scale-max 7 --decimals 2 --decimals-sd 2 --data-type likert

consequence.explanation: These two cells are the Positive/Unambiguous pair whose contrast, F(1, 94) = 92.47, is the evidence for the claim that positive-mood participants assimilate normally when the similarity cue is unambiguous.

findings.plain: If twelve people each pick a whole number from 1 to 7, only certain combinations of average and spread are arithmetically possible. Two cells of the paper's Table 2 report a spread that no such set of twelve answers can produce. Two independent pieces of software agree. The averages themselves are all fine, so this is a narrow problem with two numbers rather than a table-wide one -- but those two cells are the evidence for one of Experiment 3's conclusions.

findings.title: Experiment 4's cognitive-load means run in the opposite direction to the sentence citing them
findings.location: Experiment 4, Cognitive load conditions
findings.reported: "This pattern was identical to the neutral mood condition, in which upward comparison led to more positive self-ratings (M = 3.33, SD = 1.05), F(1,124) = 18.83, p < .001, and downward comparison led to less positive self-ratings (M = 5.53, SD = .87), F(1,124) = 7.84, p = .006, relative to the control condition." The control mean is given twice in the same section as M = 4.20, SD = .21.
findings.computed: No arithmetic performed. The passage describes 3.33 as more positive than a control of 4.20 and 5.53 as less positive than it, which reverses the printed ordering of both values against the control mean stated in the same paragraph. Values confirmed identical in the XML full text and the PDF.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The likeliest explanation by a wide margin is a transposition: swapping the two means makes the sentence internally consistent, matches the direction of all six other Experiment 4 cells, and matches the claimed parallel with the positive/load cells (5.71 upward, 3.09 downward). Nothing printed decides which of the two readings is the real one.
findings.reproduction: No command applies: this is a cross-reference contradiction between the prose and the means printed beside it, not a calculation.

consequence.explanation: Experiment 4 concludes that under cognitive load positive-mood participants behave identically to neutral-mood participants; as printed, the neutral/load means run opposite to every other cell in the experiment and so do not support the claim they are cited for.

findings.plain: In Experiment 4 the authors write that one group rated themselves more positively than a comparison group and another rated themselves less positively. The actual numbers printed in that sentence say the reverse: the supposedly higher score is 3.33 against a benchmark of 4.20, and the supposedly lower score is 5.53. Swapping the two would fix the sentence, and that is probably what happened -- but as published, the sentence Experiment 4's conclusion rests on is contradicted by the numbers inside it.

findings.title: Experiment 3 reports two manipulation-check means of 7.33 on measures whose response scales it never states
findings.location: Experiment 3, Manipulation check and Procedure
findings.reported: "the upward comparison target was rated more attractive (M = 7.33, SD = 1.19) than the downward target (M = 4.17, SD = 1.19), F(1,88) = 170.34, p < .001" and, in the same section, "Participants in the positive mood condition were more positive (M = 7.33, SD = .86) than the neutral condition (M = 5.44, SD = .97)." The Procedure says only "participants rated their own attractiveness (on the seam measures used in Experiments 1 and 2). Then, participants rated the target on her attractiveness."
findings.computed: grim_check: on the seven-point scale of Experiments 1 and 2 ("rated their own attractiveness and the target's attractiveness on seven-point scales (1 = not at all attractive and 7 = extremely attractive)"), the maximum attainable total at n = 48 is 336, while a mean of 7.33 requires 352 -- out of range. Cross-checked with R scrutiny, which returns GRIM-consistent: scrutiny tests granularity only and does not test scale bounds, so the two engines are answering different questions and this is not a disagreement about the arithmetic.
findings.assumptions: The seven-point ceiling reaches Experiment 3 only through the paper's own cross-reference, and that cross-reference sentence is attached to the SELF rating -- the target rating follows in a separate sentence carrying no scale at all. Experiment 3 demonstrably uses nine-point items for its similarity index, so a silent switch to nine-point attractiveness and mood items is a live innocent reading, and it is supported by the fact that Experiment 3's two means straddle 5.75 while the corresponding pairs in Experiments 1, 2 and 4 straddle 4. The paper is SILENT on which is true, so no out-of-range verdict is asserted here; what is asserted is that the reader cannot tell. Note also that the sentence establishing the scale contains a typo ("seam" for "same"), one of four garbled constructions in load-bearing passages, along with "rated more attractive than the (M = 5.58, SD = .78) than the unattractive target", "under cognitive loaded", and "Fours studies examine".
findings.reproduction: metascience grim --mean 7.33 --n 48 --scale-min 1 --scale-max 7 --decimals 2 --data-type likert --bound-source assumed --discreteness-source stated

consequence.explanation: Experiment 3's two manipulation checks -- that the mood induction worked and that the attractive target was seen as more attractive -- cannot be evaluated at all, because the paper does not state the scales those means are on.

findings.plain: Experiment 3 reports two average scores of exactly 7.33: one for how attractive people rated a photo, one for their own mood. If those were measured on the 1-to-7 scale the paper points back to, a 7.33 average is off the top of the scale and impossible. But Experiment 3 never actually states what scale it used for either measure, and it does use a 1-to-9 scale elsewhere, on which 7.33 is unremarkable. So this is either an impossible number or an unreported change of instrument -- and the paper gives the reader no way to tell which.

findings.title: Two contrasts presented as significant in the main text fail the authors' own Tukey correction, disclosed only in footnotes
findings.location: Experiment 2 footnote 2 and Experiment 4 footnote 5 (recovered from the PDF; absent from the XML full text)
findings.reported: "with the only difference being that in the negative mood, shared birthday, upward comparison condition differs from the control at the p = .07 level" and "with the only difference being that the high load, neutral mood induction, downward comparison condition differed from the control at the p = .13 level". Both corresponding main-text sentences assert the contrast as significant with no qualifier.
findings.computed: No arithmetic performed: this is the paper's own disclosure read against its own Results text. Separately, multiplicity_report over Experiment 4's eight cell-versus-control contrasts returned `consistent` with 0 claims lost to correction, but could evaluate only the 4 whose p was printed exactly -- and the authors' Tukey HSD is stricter than any method that check applies.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. Running and reporting the correction at all is to the authors' credit, and many papers of this period did neither; what is recorded is the placement, not the analysis.
findings.reproduction: metascience multiplicity --family-label 'Experiment 4 contrasts against the hanging control' --alpha 0.05 --tests '[{"p_value":0.001,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.002,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.001,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.006,"correction_applied":"none"}]'

consequence.explanation: Two cell-versus-control contrasts asserted without qualification in the Results text cross back over alpha = .05 (to p = .07 and p = .13) under the correction the authors themselves ran and reported.

findings.plain: The authors ran a stricter version of their statistics to check whether their results survived testing many comparisons at once. Two of them did not: they moved from 'significant' to not. The authors say so honestly, but only in footnotes, while the main text presents both as significant with no caveat. A reader who did not read the footnotes would take away two conclusions the authors' own check does not support.

findings.title: Three reported p-values disagree with their own test statistics, one with no available explanation
findings.location: Pilot study Results; Experiment 3, Perceptions of similarity
findings.reported: "F(1, 42) = .27, p = .76"; "Identical effects emerged when the information was unambiguous, F(1, 94) = 1.50, p = .83."; "r(24) = .53, p = .008".
findings.computed: statcheck extracted 63 statistics and flagged 3 after rounding rescue, with 0 decision errors -- an inconsistency rate of 4.8%. Re-run at this stage: recalc_f_to_p confirms F(1, 42) = .27 gives p = .606 as printed but p = .765 at df1 = 2 (achievable interval [.761, .768]), so the printed df1 = 1 is a typo -- the paper describes a one-way ANOVA over three conditions, which has df1 = 2, and rivets_anova independently returns `consistent` on those three groups. recalc_f_to_p on F(1, 94) = 1.50 gives p = .224 (achievable interval [.2230, .2245]) against the printed .83; the tool records this as `consistent` because it flags only over-claims, and .83 is conservative.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. A 4.8% statcheck rate is unremarkable in isolation -- roughly half of clean control papers contain at least one such inconsistency -- and this must not carry weight on its own. The middle case is the one with no innocent reading I could find: .83 is not the p of F(1, 94) = 1.50 under any tail convention, and the neighbouring sentence reports F(1, 94) = .31, p = .58, whose p is correct, so .83 is not a house convention.
findings.reproduction: metascience f-to-p --f-value 1.50 --df1 1 --df2 94 --reported-p 0.83 --decimals-p 2 --decimals-f 2

consequence.explanation: None of the three crosses the alpha the paper used -- statcheck reports zero decision errors -- so no reported conclusion changes on any of them.

findings.plain: Three of the sixty-three test results in the paper have a probability value that does not match the statistic printed next to it. One is explained by a mistyped detail and one is a small discrepancy in the cautious direction. The third, where the paper reports a probability of .83 for a statistic that implies .22, has no explanation I could find. None of the three changes whether a result counts as significant.

findings.title: Two p-values printed with the decimal point missing, on tests the paper's conclusions rely on
findings.location: Experiment 1, Self-evaluations; Experiment 4, Self-evaluations
findings.reported: "Exposure to the upward comparison target led to lowered self-evaluations (M = 3.33, SD = .65) compared to the downward comparison target (M = 4.64, SD = 1.50), F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011." and "Analysis revealed the expected three-way interaction effect of load, mood, and direction of comparison on attractiveness, F(1, 110) = 11.23, p = 001."
findings.computed: No arithmetic performed. As written each value asserts a probability of one or greater, outside the range a p-value can take. The intended values are plainly .011 and .001. Confirmed identical in the XML full text and the PDF.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. This is typographic and not a claim about the data; it is recorded because of where the two errors sit, and because each removes a test from the reach of automated verification -- both were invisible to statcheck.
findings.reproduction: No command applies: this is a notation defect in the printed text, not a calculation.

consequence.explanation: Both sit on load-bearing sentences -- Experiment 1's simple effect and Experiment 4's headline three-way interaction -- so neither of those two tests can be checked by any automated p-value checker.

findings.plain: Two probability values are printed as '011' and '001', with the decimal point dropped. Read literally they are impossible values. What the authors meant is obvious, but both sit in the sentences reporting key results, and the missing dot means automated checking software skips those two tests entirely.

findings.title: Degrees of freedom on isolated tests in Experiments 1, 2 and 3 do not reconcile with the stated sample sizes
findings.location: Experiment 1 Self-evaluations; Experiment 2 Positive and Negative mood; Experiment 3 Perceptions of similarity
findings.reported: Experiment 1 reports F(1, 46) among tests otherwise at F(1, 43); Experiment 2 reports F(1, 124) among tests at F(1, 118) and F(1, 132); Experiment 3 reports all four of its correlations as r(24).
findings.computed: check_summation_batch: Experiment 1's df 46 + 2 groups = 48 against a stated N of 47; Experiment 2's df 124 + 9 groups = 133 against a stated N of 141; Experiment 3's r(24) requires n = 26, while every derivable subgroup in that experiment is a multiple of 12. In each experiment the majority of df reconcile exactly with the stated N and design, and only isolated tests do not. 3 of 3 rows inconsistent.
findings.assumptions: These are individually weak and should be read as a pattern, not as three charges. Ordinary explanations cover each in isolation: a df printed for a model other than the one described, a contrast on a pooled error term the text does not name, or plain typos. No conclusion turns on any of them, since a df off by one or two changes no p-value materially.
findings.reproduction: metascience summation --values 24,2 --expected-sum 24 --decimals 0,0 --tolerance 0 --description 'Experiment 3 correlations r(24) imply n = 26, against the 24 participants in one mood by ambiguity combination'

consequence.explanation: Each anomalous value sits under a test cited in support of a hypothesis, but a discrepancy of one or two in the degrees of freedom changes no p-value materially, so no individual conclusion turns on these.

findings.plain: Every statistical test carries a number that encodes how many people were in it. In each of three experiments, most of those numbers add up correctly against the stated sample size and a few do not -- for example, four correlations in Experiment 3 imply 26 participants where every group in that study is a multiple of twelve. Individually these are the kind of slip that happens in any paper; together they are the same signature as the much larger sample discrepancy in Experiment 4.

findings.title: Table 1's caption names three dependent measures; the table reports one and the text reports none of the other two
findings.location: Table 1 caption versus Table 1 body (Experiment 2)
findings.reported: "Effects of upward (more attractive) versus downward (less attractive) comparisons on self-evaluations, ratings of target similarity, and use of information to benefit the self as a function of mood and shared birthday information". The table body contains a single data row, Self-evaluation.
findings.computed: No arithmetic performed. Confirmed in both sources: the XML grid has one data row and the PDF's Table 1 (page 9) likewise. Experiment 2's Dependent measures section describes only attractiveness and mood ratings, so neither 'ratings of target similarity' nor 'use of information to benefit the self' is described as collected either.

This paper reports a pilot study and four between-subjects laboratory experiments arguing that people in a positive mood reinterpret ambiguous information about a comparison target in whatever way flatters them: assimilating to someone more attractive, contrasting away from someone less attractive. It is published under a RETRACTED ARTICLE title prefix, but neither the XML nor the PDF carries a retraction notice or statement of grounds, so the reason for retraction could not be read from the article. Nothing below assumes it. Every finding rests on values printed in the paper itself.

## What actually verified

Of 41 checks that ran, 28 passed, 20 of them collapsed inside a single table check and therefore invisible in the findings list. All eight Table 2 self-evaluation means are attainable as integer totals over twelve responses on a 1-7 scale and all lie within the scale bounds. No (mean, SD) pair recurs across the two tables of summary statistics drawn from different participants, which is exactly the configuration a duplication check exists for and it came back clean. Experiment 4's control-condition SD of .21 sits comfortably inside the plausible bound for a seven-point scale under both the SD and SE readings. The pilot's self-evaluation ANOVA reconciles cleanly on the same three groups and the same assumed group sizes as the mood ANOVA that does not -- which is what shows the method, not the assumption, is producing that flag. Nothing could be refused for want of a precondition; the refusal count for this paper is zero.

## Why the pilot ANOVA leads

The mood test that opens the paper, F(2, 42) = 18.44, cannot come from the three means and SDs in the same sentence. The achievable range is [26.01, 27.04] at equal group sizes, and I re-ran it at 12/21/12 and again at 9/27/9 specifically to check whether the equal-n assumption was doing the work. It is not: the reported value sits below all three intervals, and none of 5,000 Monte Carlo draws over the rounding box reaches it. The direction is worth stating plainly, because it cuts against the obvious suspicion -- the printed statistic is *less* significant than the data imply, which is the opposite of what a self-serving error looks like. A single mistyped SD would explain it, and so would an F carried over from another analysis.

## The pattern the individual findings share

Taken one at a time, most of what follows is ordinary. A 4.8% statcheck rate is unremarkable; roughly half of clean control papers contain at least one such inconsistency. Two dropped decimal points are typographic. A caption naming measures the table does not carry is most likely copied from the other table. Degrees of freedom off by one or two change no conclusion.

What makes the set worth a reader's attention is that in each experiment the *majority* of degrees of freedom reconcile exactly with the stated N and design, and only isolated tests do not -- and in Experiment 4 that same arithmetic fails by 60 people, 31% of the sample, with no exclusions, attrition or missing data reported anywhere. The check that produces that number reconciles to the digit in Experiments 1, 2 and 3. This is the finding with the widest reach in the paper: every Experiment 4 test runs on a subset roughly two-thirds the size of the sample the paper claims.

## Two things the paper does not let a reader settle

Experiment 3 reports two manipulation-check means of exactly 7.33, one for target attractiveness and one for mood. On the seven-point scale the Procedure cross-references, 7.33 is off the top of the scale and unattainable. But that cross-reference is attached to the self-rating; the target rating follows in a separate sentence with no scale at all, Experiment 3 uses nine-point items for its similarity index, and its two attractiveness means straddle 5.75 where the corresponding pairs in the other three experiments straddle 4. I dropped this a rung from the sweep's grading for that reason. The defect that survives is not an impossible number -- it is that Experiment 3 does not state its own response scales, so neither of its manipulation checks can be evaluated at all.

The second is Experiment 4's cognitive-load paragraph, which describes 3.33 as more positive than a control of 4.20 and 5.53 as less positive than it. A transposition explains it completely, matches the direction of all six other cells in that experiment, and matches the parallel the sentence claims. Nothing printed decides it, and as published the sentence carrying Experiment 4's conclusion is contradicted by the numbers inside it.

## On effect sizes, and on the footnotes

The paper reports no effect size for any of its 63 tests and no power analysis for any of its four experiments, so I computed three. The two substantive outcomes come out at Hedges' g of 4.6 and 5.0, matched against g = 4.89 for the manipulation check -- which is to say, distinguishing self-ratings between conditions worked about as decisively as distinguishing a photograph of an attractive person from an unattractive one, out of cells of twelve. That is context, not a defect, and small-sample designs of this era routinely produced inflated published estimates.

Finally, credit where it is due: the authors ran a Tukey correction as a sensitivity analysis and reported honestly that two contrasts do not survive it, moving to p = .07 and p = .13. Many papers of this period did neither. What is recorded here is only the placement -- both reversals appear in footnotes while the main text asserts both contrasts as significant without qualification.

The arithmetic in this paper does not settle either way. Several of its numbers contradict each other, one substantially, and the paper withholds the per-cell sample sizes that would let a reader decide which of each contradictory pair to believe.

The pilot's self-evaluation ANOVA reconciles cleanly on the same three groups and the same assumed group sizes as the mood ANOVA that does not -- which is what shows the method, not the assumption, is producing that flag. Nothing could be refused for want of a precondition; the refusal count for this paper is zero.\n\n## Why the pilot ANOVA leads\n\nThe mood test that opens the paper, F(2, 42) = 18.44, cannot come from the three means and SDs in the same sentence. The achievable range is [26.01, 27.04] at equal group sizes, and I re-ran it at 12/21/12 and again at 9/27/9 specifically to check whether the equal-n assumption was doing the work. It is not: the reported value sits below all three intervals, and none of 5,000 Monte Carlo draws over the rounding box reaches it. The direction is worth stating plainly, because it cuts against the obvious suspicion -- the printed statistic is *less* significant than the data imply, which is the opposite of what a self-serving error looks like. A single mistyped SD would explain it, and so would an F carried over from another analysis.\n\n## The pattern the individual findings share\n\nTaken one at a time, most of what follows is ordinary. A 4.8% statcheck rate is unremarkable; roughly half of clean control papers contain at least one such inconsistency. Two dropped decimal points are typographic. A caption naming measures the table does not carry is most likely copied from the other table. Degrees of freedom off by one or two change no conclusion.\n\nWhat makes the set worth a reader's attention is that in each experiment the *majority* of degrees of freedom reconcile exactly with the stated N and design, and only isolated tests do not -- and in Experiment 4 that same arithmetic fails by 60 people, 31% of the sample, with no exclusions, attrition or missing data reported anywhere. The check that produces that number reconciles to the digit in Experiments 1, 2 and 3. This is the finding with the widest reach in the paper: every Experiment 4 test runs on a subset roughly two-thirds the size of the sample the paper claims.\n\n## Two things the paper does not let a reader settle\n\nExperiment 3 reports two manipulation-check means of exactly 7.33, one for target attractiveness and one for mood. On the seven-point scale the Procedure cross-references, 7.33 is off the top of the scale and unattainable. But that cross-reference is attached to the self-rating; the target rating follows in a separate sentence with no scale at all, Experiment 3 uses nine-point items for its similarity index, and its two attractiveness means straddle 5.75 where the corresponding pairs in the other three experiments straddle 4. I dropped this a rung from the sweep's grading for that reason. The defect that survives is not an impossible number -- it is that Experiment 3 does not state its own response scales, so neither of its manipulation checks can be evaluated at all.\n\nThe second is Experiment 4's cognitive-load paragraph, which describes 3.33 as more positive than a control of 4.20 and 5.53 as less positive than it. A transposition explains it completely, matches the direction of all six other cells in that experiment, and matches the parallel the sentence claims. Nothing printed decides it, and as published the sentence carrying Experiment 4's conclusion is contradicted by the numbers inside it.\n\n## On effect sizes, and on the footnotes\n\nThe paper reports no effect size for any of its 63 tests and no power analysis for any of its four experiments, so I computed three. The two substantive outcomes come out at Hedges' g of 4.6 and 5.0, matched against g = 4.89 for the manipulation check -- which is to say, distinguishing self-ratings between conditions worked about as decisively as distinguishing a photograph of an attractive person from an unattractive one, out of cells of twelve. That is context, not a defect, and small-sample designs of this era routinely produced inflated published estimates.\n\nFinally, credit where it is due: the authors ran a Tukey correction as a sensitivity analysis and reported honestly that two contrasts do not survive it, moving to p = .07 and p = .13. Many papers of this period did neither. What is recorded here is only the placement -- both reversals appear in footnotes while the main text asserts both contrasts as significant without qualification.\n\nThe arithmetic in this paper does not settle either way. Several of its numbers contradict each other, one substantially, and the paper withholds the per-cell sample sizes that would let a reader decide which of each contradictory pair to believe."}

headline.statement: The pilot study's headline mood test, F(2, 42) = 18.44, cannot be produced by the three means and standard deviations printed in the same sentence, which imply an F between 26.0 and 27.0 under every group-size allocation tested.
headline.evidence: "A one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) revealed that the mood manipulation significantly affected participant mood, F(2, 42) = 18.44, p < .001. Participants in the positive mood condition reported more positive mood (M = 7.20, SD = .93) that those in the control condition (M = 6.15, SD = .52) ... Participants in the negative mood condition reported more negative mood (M = 4.98, SD = .98)" (N = 45, three conditions, error df 42). Achievable F at 15/15/15: [26.01, 27.04]; at 12/21/12: [23.95, 24.93]; at 9/27/9: [21.16, 22.06]. Reported F = 18.44 lies below all three, and 0 of 5,000 Monte Carlo draws reproduce it.
headline.plain: In the study that sets up the whole paper, the authors report a test result showing their happy/sad writing task changed people's mood. Working backwards from the average scores they print in the very same sentence, that test result should have been about 26; they print 18.44. Changing how many people were assumed to be in each group does not fix it, so one of the numbers in that sentence is not the number the analysis actually produced.

findings.title: Pilot mood ANOVA F of 18.44 lies below every F achievable from the three means and SDs printed beside it
findings.location: Pilot study, Results (mood manipulation ANOVA)
findings.reported: "A one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) revealed that the mood manipulation significantly affected participant mood, F(2, 42) = 18.44, p < .001." Group means/SDs in the same passage: 7.20 (.93), 6.15 (.52), 4.98 (.98); N = 45, three conditions.
findings.computed: rivets_anova, re-run at this stage: achievable F interval [26.01, 27.04] at n = 15/15/15, with 0 of 5,000 Monte Carlo draws over the rounding box reaching 18.44. Re-run at 12/21/12 gives [23.95, 24.93] and at 9/27/9 gives [21.16, 22.06]; the reported value sits below all three. The reported p (< .001) is not refuted -- every achievable F is MORE significant than the one printed, so the direction of the discrepancy is conservative.
findings.assumptions: Cell ns are not printed. n = 15 per group follows from N = 45 across three conditions with error df 42 (= 45 - 3), and the finding was deliberately re-tested at two progressively more unequal allocations to check that the assumption is not doing the work; it is not. The two t-tests reported in the same passage, t(42) = 3.43 and t(42) = -3.80, carry df 42, i.e. they are contrasts on the ANOVA's pooled error term rather than two-sample tests -- a two-sample recomputation of them therefore does not apply and is not offered here as evidence.
findings.reproduction: metascience rivets-anova --means 7.20,6.15,4.98 --sds 0.93,0.52,0.98 --ns 15,15,15 --reported-f 18.44 --reported-p 0.001 --p-is-threshold --decimals-mean 2 --decimals-sd 2 --decimals-f 2

consequence.explanation: The pilot's claim that the mood induction worked rests on a statistic that does not follow from the data printed beside it; the significance decision itself is unaffected, since every achievable F is more extreme than the reported one.

findings.plain: The pilot study reports an average mood score for each of three groups, and then a test statistic summarising how different those three averages are. The averages and the test statistic do not match: the averages imply a value around 26, and the paper prints 18.44. This holds whether the groups were equal-sized or badly unbalanced. The mismatch runs in the direction that makes the result look weaker, not stronger, so it is not the shape an exaggeration would take -- but one of the two sets of numbers is wrong.

findings.title: Sixty of Experiment 4's 193 stated participants appear in no reported analysis, with no exclusions or attrition disclosed
findings.location: Experiment 4, Participants and design versus Results and discussion
findings.reported: "University (N = 193, 103 female) students participated in the study for monetary compensation. This experiment used a 2(mood: positive, neutral) x 2 (direction of comparison: upward vs. downward) x 2(load: load vs. no load) factorial design, with an additional no mood induction, no comparison, no load control condition." Every factorial test is reported at error df 110; every contrast against the control at df 124.
findings.computed: check_summation_batch, re-run at this stage over all four experiments. Experiment 4: error df 110 + 8 cells = 118 in the factorial, contrast df 124 + 9 groups = 133 in total, against a stated N of 193 -- a shortfall of 60, 31% of the sample. The same arithmetic reconciles EXACTLY in the other three: Experiment 1 (43 + 4 = 47), Experiment 2 (126 + 15 = 141), Experiment 3 (88 + 8 = 96). 1 of 4 rows inconsistent.
findings.assumptions: The derivation assumes the two df values come from the models the Methods describe -- a 2x2x2 factorial and single-df contrasts against a hanging control -- which is what the paper states, and is the reading under which the other three experiments reconcile to the digit. Innocent explanations that would resolve it entirely and are stated nowhere in the paper: undisclosed exclusions, listwise deletion, or a typo in the reported N.
findings.reproduction: metascience summation --values 118,15 --expected-sum 193 --decimals 0,0 --tolerance 0 --description 'Experiment 4 participants implied by ANOVA error df 110 plus control cell implied by contrast df 124, against the reported N of 193'

consequence.explanation: Every Experiment 4 test runs on a subset roughly two-thirds the size of the sample the paper says it recruited, and the paper reports no exclusions, attrition or missing data anywhere in that experiment.

findings.plain: Experiment 4 says it recruited 193 students. The technical details attached to every one of its statistical tests imply that only about 133 people were actually in those analyses. The paper never mentions anyone dropping out, being excluded, or having missing data. The same check reconciles perfectly for the paper's other three experiments, so this is not a quirk of how the tests were counted -- roughly a third of Experiment 4's participants are simply unaccounted for.

findings.title: Two Table 2 self-evaluation cells report a standard deviation no whole-number responses can produce
findings.location: Table 2, Self-evaluation row, Positive/Unambiguous columns (Experiment 3)
findings.reported: "6.58 (.52)" and "4.08 (.52)" -- the Positive/Unambiguous upward and downward cells, on a self-rated attractiveness item the paper describes as a single seven-point scale.
findings.computed: grimmer_check, re-run at this stage on both cells at n = 12: the single GRIM-consistent total (79 for 6.58, 49 for 4.08) admits no integer sum-of-squares of the required parity that rounds to SD = 0.52, under either the sample (n-1) or population (n) convention, with or without the scale bounds. R rsprite2 independently rejects both cells with 'The standard deviation is not consistent with this mean and number of observations (fails GRIMMER test)'. The two engines agree. Denominator: 4 of 24 checks across the 16 Table 2 cells were flagged; all 16 cell means pass GRIM.
findings.assumptions: The cell n of 12 is derived, not printed: N = 96 in a 2x2x2 design with error df 88 (= 96 - 8) forces 12 per cell. Severity is capped at `suspicious` rather than `impossible` because the tool's discreteness premise was left at 'assumed' -- if each participant really contributed one whole-number rating on a seven-point item, as the paper's cross-reference implies, the arithmetic would license a stronger verdict, but that premise reaches Experiment 3 by cross-reference rather than by a scale printed in that section. R's refusal is likewise capped at `indeterminate` by our wrapper, because a raised exception is not a proof of infeasibility (measured false-raise rate 16.2%); it corroborates without licensing escalation.
findings.reproduction: metascience grimmer --mean 6.58 --sd 0.52 --n 12 --scale-min 1 --scale-max 7 --decimals 2 --decimals-sd 2 --data-type likert

consequence.explanation: These two cells are the Positive/Unambiguous pair whose contrast, F(1, 94) = 92.47, is the evidence for the claim that positive-mood participants assimilate normally when the similarity cue is unambiguous.

findings.plain: If twelve people each pick a whole number from 1 to 7, only certain combinations of average and spread are arithmetically possible. Two cells of the paper's Table 2 report a spread that no such set of twelve answers can produce. Two independent pieces of software agree. The averages themselves are all fine, so this is a narrow problem with two numbers rather than a table-wide one -- but those two cells are the evidence for one of Experiment 3's conclusions.

findings.title: Experiment 4's cognitive-load means run in the opposite direction to the sentence citing them
findings.location: Experiment 4, Cognitive load conditions
findings.reported: "This pattern was identical to the neutral mood condition, in which upward comparison led to more positive self-ratings (M = 3.33, SD = 1.05), F(1,124) = 18.83, p < .001, and downward comparison led to less positive self-ratings (M = 5.53, SD = .87), F(1,124) = 7.84, p = .006, relative to the control condition." The control mean is given twice in the same section as M = 4.20, SD = .21.
findings.computed: No arithmetic performed. The passage describes 3.33 as more positive than a control of 4.20 and 5.53 as less positive than it, which reverses the printed ordering of both values against the control mean stated in the same paragraph. Values confirmed identical in the XML full text and the PDF.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The likeliest explanation by a wide margin is a transposition: swapping the two means makes the sentence internally consistent, matches the direction of all six other Experiment 4 cells, and matches the claimed parallel with the positive/load cells (5.71 upward, 3.09 downward). Nothing printed decides which of the two readings is the real one.
findings.reproduction: No command applies: this is a cross-reference contradiction between the prose and the means printed beside it, not a calculation.

consequence.explanation: Experiment 4 concludes that under cognitive load positive-mood participants behave identically to neutral-mood participants; as printed, the neutral/load means run opposite to every other cell in the experiment and so do not support the claim they are cited for.

findings.plain: In Experiment 4 the authors write that one group rated themselves more positively than a comparison group and another rated themselves less positively. The actual numbers printed in that sentence say the reverse: the supposedly higher score is 3.33 against a benchmark of 4.20, and the supposedly lower score is 5.53. Swapping the two would fix the sentence, and that is probably what happened -- but as published, the sentence Experiment 4's conclusion rests on is contradicted by the numbers inside it.

findings.title: Experiment 3 reports two manipulation-check means of 7.33 on measures whose response scales it never states
findings.location: Experiment 3, Manipulation check and Procedure
findings.reported: "the upward comparison target was rated more attractive (M = 7.33, SD = 1.19) than the downward target (M = 4.17, SD = 1.19), F(1,88) = 170.34, p < .001" and, in the same section, "Participants in the positive mood condition were more positive (M = 7.33, SD = .86) than the neutral condition (M = 5.44, SD = .97)." The Procedure says only "participants rated their own attractiveness (on the seam measures used in Experiments 1 and 2). Then, participants rated the target on her attractiveness."
findings.computed: grim_check: on the seven-point scale of Experiments 1 and 2 ("rated their own attractiveness and the target's attractiveness on seven-point scales (1 = not at all attractive and 7 = extremely attractive)"), the maximum attainable total at n = 48 is 336, while a mean of 7.33 requires 352 -- out of range. Cross-checked with R scrutiny, which returns GRIM-consistent: scrutiny tests granularity only and does not test scale bounds, so the two engines are answering different questions and this is not a disagreement about the arithmetic.
findings.assumptions: The seven-point ceiling reaches Experiment 3 only through the paper's own cross-reference, and that cross-reference sentence is attached to the SELF rating -- the target rating follows in a separate sentence carrying no scale at all. Experiment 3 demonstrably uses nine-point items for its similarity index, so a silent switch to nine-point attractiveness and mood items is a live innocent reading, and it is supported by the fact that Experiment 3's two means straddle 5.75 while the corresponding pairs in Experiments 1, 2 and 4 straddle 4. The paper is SILENT on which is true, so no out-of-range verdict is asserted here; what is asserted is that the reader cannot tell. Note also that the sentence establishing the scale contains a typo ("seam" for "same"), one of four garbled constructions in load-bearing passages, along with "rated more attractive than the (M = 5.58, SD = .78) than the unattractive target", "under cognitive loaded", and "Fours studies examine".
findings.reproduction: metascience grim --mean 7.33 --n 48 --scale-min 1 --scale-max 7 --decimals 2 --data-type likert --bound-source assumed --discreteness-source stated

consequence.explanation: Experiment 3's two manipulation checks -- that the mood induction worked and that the attractive target was seen as more attractive -- cannot be evaluated at all, because the paper does not state the scales those means are on.

findings.plain: Experiment 3 reports two average scores of exactly 7.33: one for how attractive people rated a photo, one for their own mood. If those were measured on the 1-to-7 scale the paper points back to, a 7.33 average is off the top of the scale and impossible. But Experiment 3 never actually states what scale it used for either measure, and it does use a 1-to-9 scale elsewhere, on which 7.33 is unremarkable. So this is either an impossible number or an unreported change of instrument -- and the paper gives the reader no way to tell which.

findings.title: Two contrasts presented as significant in the main text fail the authors' own Tukey correction, disclosed only in footnotes
findings.location: Experiment 2 footnote 2 and Experiment 4 footnote 5 (recovered from the PDF; absent from the XML full text)
findings.reported: "with the only difference being that in the negative mood, shared birthday, upward comparison condition differs from the control at the p = .07 level" and "with the only difference being that the high load, neutral mood induction, downward comparison condition differed from the control at the p = .13 level". Both corresponding main-text sentences assert the contrast as significant with no qualifier.
findings.computed: No arithmetic performed: this is the paper's own disclosure read against its own Results text. Separately, multiplicity_report over Experiment 4's eight cell-versus-control contrasts returned `consistent` with 0 claims lost to correction, but could evaluate only the 4 whose p was printed exactly -- and the authors' Tukey HSD is stricter than any method that check applies.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. Running and reporting the correction at all is to the authors' credit, and many papers of this period did neither; what is recorded is the placement, not the analysis.
findings.reproduction: metascience multiplicity --family-label 'Experiment 4 contrasts against the hanging control' --alpha 0.05 --tests '[{"p_value":0.001,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.002,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.001,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.006,"correction_applied":"none"}]'

consequence.explanation: Two cell-versus-control contrasts asserted without qualification in the Results text cross back over alpha = .05 (to p = .07 and p = .13) under the correction the authors themselves ran and reported.

findings.plain: The authors ran a stricter version of their statistics to check whether their results survived testing many comparisons at once. Two of them did not: they moved from 'significant' to not. The authors say so honestly, but only in footnotes, while the main text presents both as significant with no caveat. A reader who did not read the footnotes would take away two conclusions the authors' own check does not support.

findings.title: Three reported p-values disagree with their own test statistics, one with no available explanation
findings.location: Pilot study Results; Experiment 3, Perceptions of similarity
findings.reported: "F(1, 42) = .27, p = .76"; "Identical effects emerged when the information was unambiguous, F(1, 94) = 1.50, p = .83."; "r(24) = .53, p = .008".
findings.computed: statcheck extracted 63 statistics and flagged 3 after rounding rescue, with 0 decision errors -- an inconsistency rate of 4.8%. Re-run at this stage: recalc_f_to_p confirms F(1, 42) = .27 gives p = .606 as printed but p = .765 at df1 = 2 (achievable interval [.761, .768]), so the printed df1 = 1 is a typo -- the paper describes a one-way ANOVA over three conditions, which has df1 = 2, and rivets_anova independently returns `consistent` on those three groups. recalc_f_to_p on F(1, 94) = 1.50 gives p = .224 (achievable interval [.2230, .2245]) against the printed .83; the tool records this as `consistent` because it flags only over-claims, and .83 is conservative.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. A 4.8% statcheck rate is unremarkable in isolation -- roughly half of clean control papers contain at least one such inconsistency -- and this must not carry weight on its own. The middle case is the one with no innocent reading I could find: .83 is not the p of F(1, 94) = 1.50 under any tail convention, and the neighbouring sentence reports F(1, 94) = .31, p = .58, whose p is correct, so .83 is not a house convention.
findings.reproduction: metascience f-to-p --f-value 1.50 --df1 1 --df2 94 --reported-p 0.83 --decimals-p 2 --decimals-f 2

consequence.explanation: None of the three crosses the alpha the paper used -- statcheck reports zero decision errors -- so no reported conclusion changes on any of them.

findings.plain: Three of the sixty-three test results in the paper have a probability value that does not match the statistic printed next to it. One is explained by a mistyped detail and one is a small discrepancy in the cautious direction. The third, where the paper reports a probability of .83 for a statistic that implies .22, has no explanation I could find. None of the three changes whether a result counts as significant.

findings.title: Two p-values printed with the decimal point missing, on tests the paper's conclusions rely on
findings.location: Experiment 1, Self-evaluations; Experiment 4, Self-evaluations
findings.reported: "Exposure to the upward comparison target led to lowered self-evaluations (M = 3.33, SD = .65) compared to the downward comparison target (M = 4.64, SD = 1.50), F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011." and "Analysis revealed the expected three-way interaction effect of load, mood, and direction of comparison on attractiveness, F(1, 110) = 11.23, p = 001."
findings.computed: No arithmetic performed. As written each value asserts a probability of one or greater, outside the range a p-value can take. The intended values are plainly .011 and .001. Confirmed identical in the XML full text and the PDF.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. This is typographic and not a claim about the data; it is recorded because of where the two errors sit, and because each removes a test from the reach of automated verification -- both were invisible to statcheck.
findings.reproduction: No command applies: this is a notation defect in the printed text, not a calculation.

consequence.explanation: Both sit on load-bearing sentences -- Experiment 1's simple effect and Experiment 4's headline three-way interaction -- so neither of those two tests can be checked by any automated p-value checker.

findings.plain: Two probability values are printed as '011' and '001', with the decimal point dropped. Read literally they are impossible values. What the authors meant is obvious, but both sit in the sentences reporting key results, and the missing dot means automated checking software skips those two tests entirely.

findings.title: Degrees of freedom on isolated tests in Experiments 1, 2 and 3 do not reconcile with the stated sample sizes
findings.location: Experiment 1 Self-evaluations; Experiment 2 Positive and Negative mood; Experiment 3 Perceptions of similarity
findings.reported: Experiment 1 reports F(1, 46) among tests otherwise at F(1, 43); Experiment 2 reports F(1, 124) among tests at F(1, 118) and F(1, 132); Experiment 3 reports all four of its correlations as r(24).
findings.computed: check_summation_batch: Experiment 1's df 46 + 2 groups = 48 against a stated N of 47; Experiment 2's df 124 + 9 groups = 133 against a stated N of 141; Experiment 3's r(24) requires n = 26, while every derivable subgroup in that experiment is a multiple of 12. In each experiment the majority of df reconcile exactly with the stated N and design, and only isolated tests do not. 3 of 3 rows inconsistent.
findings.assumptions: These are individually weak and should be read as a pattern, not as three charges. Ordinary explanations cover each in isolation: a df printed for a model other than the one described, a contrast on a pooled error term the text does not name, or plain typos. No conclusion turns on any of them, since a df off by one or two changes no p-value materially.
findings.reproduction: metascience summation --values 24,2 --expected-sum 24 --decimals 0,0 --tolerance 0 --description 'Experiment 3 correlations r(24) imply n = 26, against the 24 participants in one mood by ambiguity combination'

consequence.explanation: Each anomalous value sits under a test cited in support of a hypothesis, but a discrepancy of one or two in the degrees of freedom changes no p-value materially, so no individual conclusion turns on these.

findings.plain: Every statistical test carries a number that encodes how many people were in it. In each of three experiments, most of those numbers add up correctly against the stated sample size and a few do not -- for example, four correlations in Experiment 3 imply 26 participants where every group in that study is a multiple of twelve. Individually these are the kind of slip that happens in any paper; together they are the same signature as the much larger sample discrepancy in Experiment 4.

findings.title: Table 1's caption names three dependent measures; the table reports one and the text reports none of the other two
findings.location: Table 1 caption versus Table 1 body (Experiment 2)
findings.reported: "Effects of upward (more attractive) versus downward (less attractive) comparisons on self-evaluations, ratings of target similarity, and use of information to benefit the self as a function of mood and shared birthday information". The table body contains a single data row, Self-evaluation.
findings.computed: No arithmetic performed. Confirmed in both sources: the XML grid has one data row and the PDF's Table 1 (page 9) likewise. Experiment 2's Dependent measures section describes only attractiveness and mood ratings, so neither 'ratings of target similarity' nor 'use of information to benefit the self' is described as collected either.
findings.assumptions: Because the two extra measures are absent from the Methods as well as from the table, a caption copied from another table is at least as likely as suppressed outcomes -- and Table 2 does report a Similarity row, which is where such a caption would have come from. Recorded at `suspicious` for that reason rather than as selective outcome reporting.
findings.reproduction: No command applies: this is a cross-reference contradiction between a caption and its own table.

consequence.explanation: Two dependent measures are announced in the caption of Experiment 2's only table and reported nowhere, which on its face reads as undisclosed selective outcome reporting -- though a copied caption explains it equally well.

findings.plain: The title above Experiment 2's table promises results for three different things that were measured. The table contains only one of them, and the other two are never reported anywhere in the paper. They are also not listed among the things Experiment 2 says it measured, so the likeliest explanation is that the caption was copied from the other table rather than that results were withheld.

findings.title: The only data-availability statement routes all verification through a personal request, in a paper since retracted
findings.location: Experiment 3, footnote 4 (recovered from the PDF; absent from the XML full text)
findings.reported: "Complete data and results available from the first author." No repository, accession number or supplementary file is named anywhere in the article.
findings.computed: No arithmetic performed. No supplementary files accompany this paper, so no participant-level data could be swept for duplication, and none of the paper's reported values can be checked against the data behind them.
findings.assumptions: This is the state-but-withhold pattern named in the shared rulebook, which is a standard this analysis supplies rather than one the paper accepted -- and 'available from the first author' was the ordinary convention in 2011 social psychology, so on its own it carries little weight and is not a criticism of the authors' practice at the time. It is recorded because the article is published under a RETRACTED ARTICLE title prefix, so the offer was in the event not the route to verification it appears to be.
findings.reproduction: No command applies: this is a reporting-practice observation.

consequence.explanation: No claim in the paper can be checked against the underlying data by any reader, and the single footnote offering the data is attached to Experiment 3 alone.

findings.plain: The paper offers its data only on request to one of the authors, in a single footnote, with no file or repository anyone can go to. That was normal practice for psychology in 2011 and is not a criticism of the authors by the standards of the time. It matters here only because this article has since been retracted, so that offer turned out not to be a route anyone could use.

findings.title: Every reported comparison yields an effect size near the largest the measures can express, in cells of twelve
findings.location: Experiment 2 Manipulation check; Table 2, Self-evaluation and Similarity rows (Experiment 3)
findings.reported: The paper reports no effect size for any of its 63 tests, and no a-priori power analysis for any of its four experiments.
findings.computed: check_effect_plausibility, from the group statistics the paper prints: Experiment 2's attractiveness manipulation check gives Hedges' g = 4.89 [4.22, 5.62]; Experiment 3's Positive/Ambiguous similarity contrast g = 5.03 [3.53, 6.88]; Experiment 3's Positive/Unambiguous self-evaluation contrast g = 4.64 [3.23, 6.39]. Separately, required_n: a 12-versus-12 cell pair has 46% of the sample needed to detect even a conventionally large effect (d = 0.8) at 80% power.
findings.assumptions: This is context I am supplying, not a defect the paper owed anyone. All three dispersions are labelled SD rather than SEM, all three comparisons are between-subjects as described, and no units mismatch is in play, so the three ordinary deflationary explanations are ruled out. The right yardstick is the manipulation check itself: g = 4.89 for 'is this photograph of an attractive person more attractive than this photograph of an unattractive person' is exactly where such a value is expected. The two substantive outcomes sit in the same range, which is the part worth a reader's attention. Small-sample designs of this era routinely produced inflated published estimates, and that is a property of the literature, not an accusation about this paper.
findings.reproduction: metascience effect-size --mean1 7.06 --sd1 0.53 --n1 12 --mean2 4.14 --sd2 0.59 --n2 12 --design between

consequence.explanation: Nothing the paper claims is contradicted by this; it bears on how much weight a reader should put on effect magnitudes the paper itself never reports.

findings.plain: The paper never reports how big its effects were, so I calculated them. Its substantive results are as large as its manipulation check -- the deliberately obvious comparison between an attractive and an unattractive photograph -- meaning the two groups' scores barely overlap at all. That is very unusual for measures of how people rate themselves, and it comes out of groups of twelve people, which is under half the size needed to reliably detect even a large effect. structured_output.report_markdown:
This paper reports a pilot study and four between-subjects laboratory experiments arguing that people in a positive mood reinterpret ambiguous information about a comparison target in whatever way flatters them: assimilating to someone more attractive, contrasting away from someone less attractive. It is published under a RETRACTED ARTICLE title prefix, but neither the XML nor the PDF carries a retraction notice or statement of grounds, so the reason for retraction could not be read from the article. Nothing below assumes it. Every finding rests on values printed in the paper itself.

## What actually verified

Of 41 checks that ran, 28 passed, 20 of them collapsed inside a single table check and therefore invisible in the findings list. All eight Table 2 self-evaluation means are attainable as integer totals over twelve responses on a 1-7 scale and all lie within the scale bounds. No (mean, SD) pair recurs across the two tables of summary statistics drawn from different participants, which is exactly the configuration a duplication check exists for and it came back clean. Experiment 4's control-condition SD of .21 sits comfortably inside the plausible bound for a seven-point scale under both the SD and SE readings. The pilot's self-evaluation ANOVA reconciles cleanly on the same three groups and the same assumed group sizes as the mood ANOVA that does not -- which is what shows the method, not the assumption, is producing that flag. Nothing could be refused for want of a precondition; the refusal count for this paper is zero.

## Why the pilot ANOVA leads

The mood test that opens the paper, F(2, 42) = 18.44, cannot come from the three means and SDs in the same sentence. The achievable range is [26.01, 27.04] at equal group sizes, and I re-ran it at 12/21/12 and again at 9/27/9 specifically to check whether the equal-n assumption was doing the work. It is not: the reported value sits below all three intervals, and none of 5,000 Monte Carlo draws over the rounding box reaches it. The direction is worth stating plainly, because it cuts against the obvious suspicion -- the printed statistic is *less* significant than the data imply, which is the opposite of what a self-serving error looks like. A single mistyped SD would explain it, and so would an F carried over from another analysis.

## The pattern the individual findings share

Taken one at a time, most of what follows is ordinary. A 4.8% statcheck rate is unremarkable; roughly half of clean control papers contain at least one such inconsistency. Two dropped decimal points are typographic. A caption naming measures the table does not carry is most likely copied from the other table. Degrees of freedom off by one or two change no conclusion.

What makes the set worth a reader's attention is that in each experiment the *majority* of degrees of freedom reconcile exactly with the stated N and design, and only isolated tests do not -- and in Experiment 4 that same arithmetic fails by 60 people, 31% of the sample, with no exclusions, attrition or missing data reported anywhere. The check that produces that number reconciles to the digit in Experiments 1, 2 and 3. This is the finding with the widest reach in the paper: every Experiment 4 test runs on a subset roughly two-thirds the size of the sample the paper claims.

## Two things the paper does not let a reader settle

Experiment 3 reports two manipulation-check means of exactly 7.33, one for target attractiveness and one for mood. On the seven-point scale the Procedure cross-references, 7.33 is off the top of the scale and unattainable. But that cross-reference is attached to the self-rating; the target rating follows in a separate sentence with no scale at all, Experiment 3 uses nine-point items for its similarity index, and its two attractiveness means straddle 5.75 where the corresponding pairs in the other three experiments straddle 4. I dropped this a rung from the sweep's grading for that reason. The defect that survives is not an impossible number -- it is that Experiment 3 does not state its own response scales, so neither of its manipulation checks can be evaluated at all.

The second is Experiment 4's cognitive-load paragraph, which describes 3.33 as more positive than a control of 4.20 and 5.53 as less positive than it. A transposition explains it completely, matches the direction of all six other cells in that experiment, and matches the parallel the sentence claims. Nothing printed decides it, and as published the sentence carrying Experiment 4's conclusion is contradicted by the numbers inside it.

## On effect sizes, and on the footnotes

The paper reports no effect size for any of its 63 tests and no power analysis for any of its four experiments, so I computed three. The two substantive outcomes come out at Hedges' g of 4.6 and 5.0, matched against g = 4.89 for the manipulation check -- which is to say, distinguishing self-ratings between conditions worked about as decisively as distinguishing a photograph of an attractive person from an unattractive one, out of cells of twelve. That is context, not a defect, and small-sample designs of this era routinely produced inflated published estimates.

Finally, credit where it is due: the authors ran a Tukey correction as a sensitivity analysis and reported honestly that two contrasts do not survive it, moving to p = .07 and p = .13. Many papers of this period did neither. What is recorded here is only the placement -- both reversals appear in footnotes while the main text asserts both contrasts as significant without qualification.

The arithmetic in this paper does not settle either way. Several of its numbers contradict each other, one substantially, and the paper withholds the per-cell sample sizes that would let a reader decide which of each contradictory pair to believe.
